Ralph LaLama

Tenor saxophonist Ralph LaLama was born in West Aliquippa, Pennsylvania on January 30, 1951. His big band experience includes stints with Buddy Rich, Woody Herman and the Vanguard Jazz Orchestra. Ralph has co-led a quartet with fellow saxophonist Joe Lovano and records as a leader on the Criss-Cross label.
Ralph was interviewed in Utica, New York on May 23, 2010 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe and I am off-camera for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive, and I am very pleased to be speaking with saxophonist Ralph LaLama today. Welcome back to Utica, New York.

Thank you, Monk. Yeah, it’s nice to be here. We had a good gig yesterday, two gigs, yes. People are nice around here. You know I used to play here. Tiny’s and do some concerts, and did a bunch of stuff for J.R. [Monterose], did a couple of benefits for Phyllis [Monterose], I remember with Nick [Brignola] and Joe Mags [Magnarelli] and you know Rick [Montalbano]. I remember Rick [Montalbano] Junior —
Yeah me too.
Yeah but I mean when he was tiny, man, like he would sit in with us. And yesterday he played the gigs with us.
Yeah isn’t that something?
Yeah it is funny.
It sort of makes you feel like am I that old?
Right.
I was told Utica, I’m not a native of here but I’m from Rochester, but I was told that Utica used to be like a midway point, sort of guys would travel the Thruway and —

That’s right. Come between Rochester — you know I have, I don’t know if this is part of the question but I’m going to say it here — I have an affinity here for Upstate New York because I’m from Pittsburgh and I’ve been living in New York for about 35 years. But I grew up in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. And I went to school at Youngstown State University. And why that’s relevant is there was a guy that was going to school at the time, he just got off of Woody Herman’s band, his name was Tony Leonardi. And he was from Syracuse, okay. So he grew up with Sal [Amico], he played with Chuck [Mangione] and you know he played with Joe Romano and Nick and probably J.R. too. But Tony was kind of my mentor, you know. Even though he was about eleven years older than me. And at Youngstown State he started which was at that time a one hour elective jazz band. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

It wasn’t part of the curriculum really except for it was an elective. So my point is that Tony turned me on to all kinds of great, you know he heard I played — I auditioned for the band. I didn’t know the band. I just auditioned for the band, I made it, and we started becoming with friends, and he turned me on to all these hip — then I remember he invited Sal Nistico to the school, so we could hear him, you know? And he played with us, and then I got to know Sal. Now again when I moved to New York I moved to Queens, Elmhurst Queens. And at that time Sal lived in Rego Park. And Sal was nice enough, you know, because he remembered me and he knew I was trying to play and all that stuff, and so he put me on some of his gigs, you know, like quartet gigs, he made them a quintet for little Ralphie to play. You know what I mean? Right out of school, I was in my early twenties. Because I got out of Woody Herman’s band and Sal was there, and Tony Leonardi played — you know I didn’t play with him, I mean in Woody’s band, but I mean they were alumni. Joe Romano. I met Joe, coming to New York, and then Nick I played with up here. So the only one I didn’t know that well was J.R. because he was already gone playing when I started. So I always feel like, not that this is my home, but I always felt like very close to the Upstate guys because of Tony, and then Sal, and then Joe you know, and even Chuck.
And all these Upstate guys are, you know their last name always ends with a vowel.
Yeah that’s right.
It’s something about Italians.
Well that’s it: Lovano, LaLama, you know, Nistico. Even Zito or a’s.
Very interesting. A couple of books have come out recently about that. Italian Americans in the jazz world.
That’s right. That’s true. Most definitely.

I wanted to pose a question to you. If you were able to write your own entry about yourself for a new coming jazz book, like a jazz encyclopedia, and you could actually write it yourself, you might say, “ Ralph LaLama sounds reminiscent of” blank and blank. Like two tenor players.
Oh two tenors.
Who would you pick?
I would probably have to say Sonny Rollins and Hank Mobley.
Well you know it’s interesting because the guy who wrote the entry for the Grove Encyclopedia of Jazz said exactly that.
Oh did he.

Yeah. I’m not sure of his name but I just looked in there and that’s exactly what it said, that those were like big influences on you. And I noticed yesterday, I was so pleased when you started out the concert with that Hank Mobley tune. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
Oh yeah, “Dis I Dig of You” that’s right.
Not many people — well at least in my experience — have heard that played a lot.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah, because that’s my influence. I mean you know I remember when I was growing up, I mean like jazz growing up let’s put it that way, it was in the 70s and everybody started playing like Coltrane. And I like Coltrane, I mean he’s one of my influences too, and Joe Henderson and those guys. But I was always towards the Sonny thing. And then moving to New York, I was different. Because I was trying to play like Sonny and everybody else was going Trane, you know? I don’t know, it probably helped me a little bit and hindered me a little bit. You know, because if they wanted the status quo they wouldn’t hire me, if they wanted something a little different they would hire me.
I see.
And I didn’t do that for any business reason. I just was turned on by it.
Well what, at the time, can you put into words what was the different approach, if you were more into Sonny than Trane? Less notes?

Less notes, more melody, more rhythm. I mean not that Trane didn’t play with rhythm, I don’t want to be quoted as saying that. But Sonny had a spontaneity. A melodic and rhythmic spontaneity I think compared to — Trane was more practiced. And even though, I mean it worked, you know don’t get me wrong, it’s not a put down by any means. It’s just what I was attracted to. It’s what I went towards. It’s what I like. You know you’ve got to be honest with yourself. And back in Youngstown prior to that, it’s what my father used to listen to. He used to listen to Sonny Stitt, Gene Ammons, Stan Getz. I mean I didn’t even hear Sonny Rollins and Trane at first, or even Charlie [Parker] until I met Tony. It wasn’t in the air in my house. I heart Stitt, singers, my mother was a singer, my father was a drummer. So I had music in the house, it was in the air, that’s the way I would put it. I like James Brown. You know, because you’re a kid. You know, not that I didn’t like jazz, I did. But James Brown, when you’re growing up, I mean that’s my generation. James Brown, the Temptations, you know.
And you got your rhythmic dose from that.
That’s right. Totally. From James, oh definitely. No doubt about it.
You know I think you can learn a lot, even if you’re a jazz player, from listening to what those horn players are playing behind him and all those things.

Yeah. And the rhythm section, the feeling. The feeling. James Brown — I still love it. I mean to me that’s how good it is. When I put it on now, after all I’ve been through in a musical sense, I still enjoy it as much. So to me that’s true art. That might not be in the books as art, but to me it is. Because I get a kick out of it. It’s not just nostalgic either. It’s a feeling. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
You had your big band experiences under three kind of different leaders. You had Mel Lewis and Buddy Rich and Woody Herman. Who did you enjoy the most?

Well I can’t, that’s a hard — here I could explain it in a certain way. My first band was Woody Herman and that was like my first professional jazz gig so to speak. I mean I’d played a lot of gigs, but I don’t mean professional as far as getting paid, but upper eschelons jazz. And Woody, and I just learned a lot. I learned a lot from Woody because of the fact that I finally realized that a leader has to trust you. I don’t mean just showing up on time, but the music and showing up on time, and just being there for the gig. That’s when he starts liking you, when he trusts you. And that was a big lesson. I mean it just hit me one day, oh man, that’s how you get along.
To trust you to not only play but —

Be there, and you know, just be there. But even the music too. I mean musically he has to trust you. When you go up to play, let’s say a solo, you’re going to be right. You know? I’m not saying you can’t make a mistake, I mean it’s just the attitude. And okay, and then I went to Buddy Rich and I really enjoyed that too. Well Buddy was a lunatic but still he was a real musician. I’m not totally agreeable when I hear all these stories. Not that they weren’t true, but his attitude really wasn’t like — he was a musician, you know what I mean? And he wanted things right. I can tell you a couple of stories. I remember one time the whole trumpet section was gone and they hired all these guys from North Texas State. And they really weren’t up to snuff. I mean they couldn’t handle — and we all figured oh Buddy, he’s going to go crazy. He didn’t say a word. He just fired them. He gave them their two weeks notice. You know why? Because he knew they weren’t that talented. But he would holler at you if he knew you were talented and you weren’t doing the job, you know? So I respected him. You know what I mean? And I remember another time he invited Mel Lewis to the band because he couldn’t even get dressed, he had this back problem with his discs. He couldn’t get dressed, right? So I remember they had to help him get dressed. He would get dressed on the bus. But I remember Mel was there for a week but didn’t play one beat. Because Buddy would, after all that pain — I mean I saw this guy was in pain. You know when somebody is in pain, they’re not faking it you know. So he would go up there and play. And then he’d go back, and he was in pain. So he had Mel Lewis there, but Mel didn’t play a note. Okay now in London I ended up, we were there for a month, we were at Ronnie Scott’s for a week but I got sick, I had the flu, I had to go to the doctor, you know, I mean I had a 103 temperature. I had a terrible flu. And Steve Marcus and Andy Fusco went into Buddy’s room and said, “Buddy, man, Ralph is sick, I mean I don’t know if he can play.” And he goes, “Is he dead?” They said, “No.” And then so I’m on the bandstand and I played and I think he called almost every tune I played on too. Okay. But you know what? If you tell that story out of context that © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
sounds like Buddy’s not a very nice human being. But I could dig him because when he was sick he played. Even though he had a sub, he had Mel Lewis on the bus. Mel didn’t play one note.
So he wouldn’t ask you do to anything that he wouldn’t do.

That’s right. That’s what I got from him. You know what I mean? So to me that’s what I mean, I mean he’s crazy but I could dig it. I mean technically, on that band you played much more notes. I don’t mean complicated but for me as a saxophone player I learned a lot about the saxophone technique because of some of the music he played. It was like hard, another step. Okay? And then with Mel and Thad, when I got to New York, I mean I knew Thad. I met Thad at Youngstown. Tony Leonardi got Thad to come to Youngstown. So I used to sub on the band. My first gig in New York was with Mel and Thad, but it wasn’t the big band, it was a quintet. So that flipped me out. That was my first gig.
You said something yesterday, you said you learned more on that gig on the first few weeks than you did in college. What do you learn on that first — I mean what was so memorable?

Well just what the thing sounded like around you. You know, and how they handled, I mean these were masters of playing jazz music. And I’m just out of college. And Tony Leonardi was great, believe me, I mean I learned a lot from him. But now this is experiencing it. That’s what I mean. Even with now you say about the band with Thad and Mel or the Mel Lewis band, that was more like real life. I mean he dealt with a lot — you know it’s in your home town which is now New York, you go to work and just the music was so ridiculously challenging at the time especially, and you’re with Thad Jones and Mel Lewis and everybody else in the band, when I was subbing, it was Pepper Adams, you know Jerry Dodgion, you know what I mean? All these guys. I said what? Bob Brookmeyer. You know I mean I’m a kid. So for a summation, and I don’t want to make this sound weird, because it’s not like this, but just to compare it I would say Woody was like high school, Buddy was like college, and Mel was like life. You know what I mean? That’s the way I would answer your question, even though it took me a half hour to answer your question.
That’s okay. I like long answers. I don’t know if I can phrase this question correctly, but in improvisation, in jazz improvisation, to you, what constitutes a wrong note?

Well okay that’s a good question. It’s like beauty is in the eyes of the beholder, okay? I think there are wrong notes. A lot of people don’t. I do. I really do. Because you have a background, you have a chord, and then you could use all twelve notes but it’s how you organize them. You know what I mean? It’s the organization. Sometimes you might put a wrong note in a wrong part of the beat or something, and it sounds wrong. And I just get © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

this tension up my spine. You know what I mean? But, then technically you can play a wrong note, technically meaning theoretically it could be a wrong note but it sounds right. You know, because of the placement. You know Thad Jones was the master of it. Coltrane too. Sonny Rollins, all those masters, Joe Henderson. As far as theoretically, in other words we have a chord, we have a scale and we have the chord tone. So if you play outside of that, it could be considered wrong. But if you know how to phrase it exactly right and resolve it right that’s another thing. It’s in the resolution. You can resolve a wrong note and make it right see. And then sometimes I know when I hit a wrong note, you know like I say I feel it up my spine, and I usually hear it from my wife.
Are you joking?
No. My wife is a great singer, Nicole Pasternak, she’s a great singer.
Okay.

And she has great ears too. You know what I mean? But I’m just saying I’m joking but I’m not. I’m serious about what I’m saying. But she doesn’t actually holler at me, but I know she can tell when I hit it. But when you’re trying to improvise, sometimes you get hung up. So if you just play all your licks that are comfortable, all your stuff, then you’re not going to mess up. Then I don’t think you’re really improvising. You know what I mean? I mean like Monk. Monk. Speaking of Monk, [scats] it’s obviously — not a wrong note — but it sounds right. It sounds — there’s tension. Let’s put it this way: there’s tension notes, and there’s wrong notes. Ah that’s very good Ralph.
We’ll quote you on that. You’ll make our little snippets of good quotes.
Yeah.
But I noticed yesterday in listening to you —
A lot of wrong notes.
Well no, every once in a while you would end a phrase with a note that made me go, like literally, like gee I wish I would have thought of that. But it sounded pretty cool.

Well that’s what I mean. That was tension. That wasn’t wrong, hopefully. You know what I mean? I mean that’s the way I would interpret it. I don’t know, I’ve been doing that a lot more lately. I’ve been trying to get a little bit more modern. I don’t know, I don’t like that term, but in other words I’m just experimenting. And hopefully if all these improvisers do, you know, you don’t want to be complacent. I don’t. That’s boring to me. So I started a very concrete — but that’s not the — consonant, I was more consonant when I first started playing. Well this was actually a lot of my upstate influence. You know what I mean? And as I got older and you know you start hearing more, and you hear other guys too, I get influenced by other people too. I’ll be honest about that. I’m definitely influenced by what things are around me at the moment and at different places and in different cultures. Because I’m lucky, I get to go around the world. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
You’ve spent some time in Italy right?
Oh yeah.
What do you do there?

Well I do some teaching over there and actually with the Vanguard band we go once a year to Assisi, where we play a couple of concerts and we also do clinics, you know? And at one time I did something for the Manhattan School of Music, about five years in a row, we went to a place close to Venice, it was called Tuscafarco, and we were there for two weeks, all teaching and playing too, playing too, concerts. The faculty played at night and then we taught all day for two weeks. I did that for about five years in a row. That was nice, yeah. And then other times, just go there, in spots. I went to Spain, did a couple of clinics there on my own, and I mean with the bands too. I go with the Vanguard band, we’ll do clinics individually and in sections sometimes.
Do the people over there — I don’t know if “respect” is the right word — do they think of jazz as more significant than here?

Yeah. Because this is our gift to them. This is the only original art form that America has to offer. Original art form. I mean rock & roll is not original, it’s not American. You know classical music is not original. I mean there’s a lot of American composers but they’re not original. I mean they might be original in their own music but I’m saying the idea of classical music is not American. The idea of jazz is American, it’s an original American art form. So this is our gift to Japan, our gift to Germany. And a lot of people try to copy it. So yeah I would say they respect it. Oh yeah. Definitely. Totally.
You had a statement yesterday, actually just to follow-up on rock & roll, do you have an issue with the way people behave?

Oh, that’s right. You know I don’t know why I said that but it’s true. You know it used to make me mad. You know, these little old Puerto Rican ladies who had to clean up this mess that these guys I mean they didn’t have to break bottles. I mean I party too — oh it’s my phone, where is my phone.
That’s all right, we can edit this tape.
You know what, I’m not going to even answer it. I don’t know who that is. I’ll shut it off.
I’ll bet I know who it was. We were talking about rock & roll, it was probably Eric Clapton calling you “Ralph, what are you doing next week?”
“I can’t make it.”
Okay. So we were talking about rock & roll, and the behavior that sometimes is associated with that music.

And I guess I just — would you appreciate it? If your mother had to clean up? I mean because I spent a lot of time in hotel rooms. And I’m not saying, I mean I party but I don’t break glass and I just think these guys — it’s disrespectful. And sometimes the © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

music sounds that way to me. Not everybody. I mean I love Jimi Hendrix, you know, I loved a lot of people when I was growing up especially, that had something to say. You know? And I’m not against that, not at all. I love James Taylor, I mean that’s not rock & roll, but you know. Who was the other — Laura Nyro, Carole King, yeah, and Jimi Hendrix. I loved Jimi Hendrix. But I didn’t like Cream that much. But I liked Jimi Hendrix you know what I mean?
You don’t have to like everybody I guess.
Yeah.

And speaking of learning, I have this thing that came to me yesterday when you were playing, and it has something to do with teaching I think, because I mean you can learn the Real Book tunes and all that, but there was stuff that you guys did yesterday that I was wondering where it came from. And one of example was you did the tune “Like Someone In Love.” And near the end of it, right at the end, you played a lick, it was sort of a tag, and it sounded like: “My mama done told me.”
Exactly right. That’s my Woody influence.
So where does that come from and how do you, as a teacher, get your kids to learn all that?

That’s my experience. That’s where that came from. I didn’t think about it. We used to play it in Woody’s band: “My mama done told me/to bring home the” you know whatever the words. You know, “Blues in the Night.” And then when you live the stuff, see that’s what I mean, when you live the stuff, see that’s what I mean, when you learn it in the Real Book sometimes you’re not living it unless you play it for a couple of years, you know, a song let’s say. And that’s all. And that came to my mind, because that was part of my musical growing up, you know?
Okay. So that thing wasn’t an outtro so to speak that I should have known about?
No.
Okay, you just — it sounded just like it was part of it.
But it fit. I try to be melodic, musical. Yeah, that’s right. Yeah, you’ve got to make all this fit. And that’s through experience you know?
Yeah, but there was a couple of other things too, like some intros and stuff that you don’t see in the Real Book.
Yeah they’re not there.
I guess that as a teacher you may pass those on to your students.

I might show them different ways they can go with things. The reason why I would do that, not that they would copy me, they maybe copy me for a little bit but mainly so that they realize they have the freedom to do that, to use their own ingenuity, their own creativeness. You don’t have to just read it like a book. You know there’s a lot of people © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

when they learn from the Real Books and stuff, they think oh we have to do it like the book. But the book says that. No it’s not. I mean that’s not The Bible. All it is is a guide. That’s the same way you play chord changes. You know because it says this doesn’t mean you can’t use that, you know, but it has to sound right. That’s what I mean. That’s where taste comes in. You know? And tension and all. Ahhh.
You know what, you can use that when you go back and teach.
Well I do, I think I do. But I’ll even use it more because it makes more sense now.
Speaking of the Real Book and the number of tunes in it that date back to the Great American Songbook —
Oh sure.
How come? How come those songs that were not really written as jazz tunes per se offer such a rich palette of —

Well because you said it. Because the songs really, you can improvise on them. They’re made perfectly to improvise. You see, I don’t want to get too technical, but to me improvising is about tension to release. You have a tension and you release it, in other words you resolve it. Okay? And even when you don’t resolve it, the tension is, like you said, it’s up in the air, to be resolved. And that’s all right too. And a lot of these American Songbooks have that. They have the tension to the release. And to put it in musical, in theoretical terms, it’s the dominant to the tonic. And these tunes that we were talking about, like they might be in one key but within that form you go to about five keys. What does that mean? You have to have the tension to the release. The tension to the release. Tension to the release. So that’s perfect for a jazzer, they want to deal with it, to improvise. It’s like putting a carrot in front of a rabbit. You know?
Well do you find it harder than, or a different kind of challenge to improvise like on a tune like “So What,” where you’ve just got two chords and they’re just —

Um hum. Exactly. I understand what you mean. Well to me it’s almost sometimes harder. For me. Because I mean just for the fact, well the more I study music the more I realize how many tensions are in there. See? At first I just looked at it as one thing. The Dorian mode let’s say. But no, it’s more than that. You start learning how you could — that’s the foundation. You could learn how you start building upon it. And I’m still working on that. Thinking about that. And then you could relate that to other songs too. See that’s what guys are doing today. They’re taking their modal kind of things and putting it on these standards. And inside the tension to the release. You know what I’m saying? I don’t want to get too technical, but that’s simple I think. That’s just tension to release. So you could add tension to that long 16 bars of D Dorian, and you can look at it a lot of different ways. But at first, to me, all that space made it much harder for me. For me. Not the rest of the world. That came from the Upstate, Tony Leonardi school, and Sal Nistico, © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

change-change-change-change-change-change. And which I loved. But I’m saying but then when I got to “So What” I said what do I do? D Dorian for eighteen thousand years. And then it goes up a half step. But you know, but I mean, but to me they’re both great. But yeah, it does present a challenge, because that’s hard to resolve with all that movement with keys in the Songbook, that’s hard too. Because you’ve got to know your keys. But you’ve got to know your keys when you’re talking about superimposition on the Dorian mode. See? So it’s all the same.
Is there a short list of things that you really want your students to be able to do by the time they move on?
Oh sure.
And what might be a couple of them?

Well play in time. Have a good tone. Play in time with the rhythm, not just rhythmically correct but the harmonic rhythm, the harmonic rhythm. That means like when you’re playing these standards or playing the modal stuff, you’re playing the harmony it has to have, the rhythm of the harmony has to resolve in the right places. Because there’s corny places to resolve, and there’s hip places to resolve. You know what I’m saying? So and not to get too into it, but that’s my criteria. You’ve got to learn how to do that, if you want to be my student. You know, and that’s great, they love it because now it starts to make sense what they’re playing.
What method do you use in a lesson? Do you play chords with them?

Sometimes. Sometimes I play on saxophone. If they don’t hear it I go to the piano and say you’re playing this note. I’ll play the chord and say, “Here’s the note you landed on.” And they say, “Oh yeah. Now I know what you mean by wrong and tension.” There it goes again.
Well along the similar lines, what makes things individually or as a rhythm section, what makes things swing?
Ooh. What makes things swing. Well it’s feeling. Hmm how could I say it. You mean technically what makes things swing?

If you were listening to a rhythm section or you were on one of those gigs just like this weekend where you get with a group and you can tell right after the first couple of times, well this band really swings, or this thing does not really swing. Is it possible to put that into words.

Yeah okay well I’ll try, now I’m understanding you better. To me, when people play together more, they’re in the same thought zone, that usually swings. And not that all swinging is the same, but it usually gets off the ground, I like to put it. You know what I mean? And it’s magic that happens. And that’s usually swinging. You know what I mean? Now the technical thing is the way they play the eighth notes. In other words, © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

some guys, I know I have a lot of students that come in out of high school and they think swinging is [scats]. To me you’re putting two eighth notes like more like a dotted eighth and a sixteenth. And that’s not it. It’s more of a triplet. [scats]. So that’s the technical thing. And it’s not just the drummer and the bass player, it’s also the horn players too. [scats]. That’s not it. So that adds to the not-swing. And why it’s not swing is because one guy is maybe swinging and the other guy’s going [scats] so that’s not together. So as a band that’s not happening. It’s not gelling. It’s not magic. You know what I mean? It’s not getting off the ground. It’s not leaving the earth. Okay? But when it is leaving the earth — the same with a funk band, if you’re a great funk band it’s the same thing. Boy they’re so together. You know? It lifts you right off the ground, you know what I mean? And a symphony orchestra. When it’s totally together, it’s swinging man. You know what I’m saying? It’s not swinging — that’s not what I’m talking about. I’m talking about togetherness. You know? And the world can learn a lot from that too. And politicians can learn a lot from that. The democrats and the republicans can learn a lot about that, doing it together. You know what I mean? Not I say black you say orange. I say furnace you say snowflake.
I thought of this question when you said your wife was a singer. Do you play a melody of a tune differently if it has a well-known lyric?

You know ever since I’ve been married, yes. I mean now I know a lot of the words, I’m not going to lie to you and say I studied the words, even though Lester Young did and a lot of people do.
